MR. DOUGLAS-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "PROVINCE" RESPECTING FRAUDULENT VOTING
speechtext:
rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, affecting the members of this party who represent constituencies in British Columbia. My specific question of privilege relates to an article which appeared in the Vancouver Province of February 22, written by Mr. Ormond Turner. This copy of the Vancouver Province only came to my hand this morning. I am therefore raising this matter at the very earliest opportunity that was practicable.
The article reads in part as follows:
A local union official has privately admitted that at least six B.C. unions have conspired to get N.D.P. candidates elected fraudulently by entering fictitious names on the voters' lists.

subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "PROVINCE" RESPECTING FRAUDULENT VOTING
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "PROVINCE" RESPECTING FRAUDULENT VOTING
speechtext:
The article continues:
He said that union members (and others) then went to the polls and used the phony names to help elect N.D.P. candidates.
He didn't seem proud to have been involved in this illegal and shocking subversion of Canada's election laws; he agreed that a conspiracy to fraudulently affect the outcome of an election was an affront to democracy-no matter what the candidate stood for.
Here's how it works;
A union hiring hall in Vancouver gets a call for 25 men to go to a job at Nanaimo . .. While there an election is called and registration begins. The 25 workers are registered at Nanaimo (quite legally) but, by the time the election day comes around, they have either returned to Vancouver or gone on to another construction site. There are 49 days set aside for registration and they could be registered anew at each site, often without their knowledge. Remember, when the enumerator comes around, you can be registered by the landlady.
At each site a list is kept by the local union giving the names and addresses used in the registrations. On election day, some one casts these votes. Some of the names are fictitious, some have phony addresses, some are legitimate-but there is no doubt that illegal votes are cast.
In every riding where this has been proved to happen, the NJD.P. has benefited, with or without that party's knowledge.
20220-738J
I shall quote one other sentence in which the writer says:
-the evidence I've got weighs about three pounds. It's conclusive, it's shocking, and it will provide a good deterrent to anyone who intends to play around with our form of democracy at the next election.
I shall be quite prepared, Mr. Speaker, to place with the Clerk a full copy of the article because I have not taken the time of the house to read all of it. This article casts a serious reflection upon the trade unions in the province of B.C., and calls in question the legality of the election of certain members of this party.
The president of the international woodworkers of America, who drew this to my attention, has written me a letter a copy of which I shall also place with the Clerk. It is dated February 22, addressed to me, and says:
Please find enclosed a press clipping from the Vancouver Province of February 22, 1965 written by one Ormond Turner in which he, by inference, accuses trade unions in the province of British Columbia of conspiring to elect fraudulently members of the New Democratic party.
I am alarmed at these accusations because our union, the international woodworkers of America, being the largest in the province of British Columbia and having a social and political policy at this time of supporting the New Democratic party, and because our policy is so well known to the general public may be tainted by these innuendoes and accusations.
If any unions did indeed, conspire to fraudulently elect anyone I would like to know what unions and which officers did such conspiring. If there is any truth-which I sincerely doubt-in these accusations, then it is only fair that the public and the government know who and which organizations are involved.
It is quite true that there may be duplications of some of our members in federal elections; but this would come about mainly among their transient loggers who could be resident in one of the Vancouver ridings but who at the time of an election gets a call for work in one of the up-coast logging operations and, as there is no absentee voting in federal elections, must either register in the up-coast camp and vote in that riding or be denied a vote. We have always encouraged our members to vote, regardless of who they wish to vote for.
If it can be proven that someone has cast a ballot in a Vancouver riding under the name of an I.W.A. member who legitimately votes in a up-coast riding, then I for one want to know who would perpetrate such an unscrupulous act and on whose behalf it was done. We in the I.W.A. have long recognized that democracy can

Question of Privilege
only work if the people elected to represent various ridings are elected by the majority of votes legitimately cast on their behalf; and -we will strongly deplore any individual or group in society who would attempt to rig elections-whether they be union elections, federal, provincial or municipal elections.
Because of the fact that trade unions have been accused in public of nefarious deeds and because of the fact that so much is at stake, I would request that you do whatever you can to have this whole matter turned over to the proper authorities so that either the culprits (if they exist) are exposed by name, or these scurrilous accusations are publicly laid to rest.
Fraternally yours,
J. A. Moore, President.
I agree wholeheartedly with the sentiments expressed by Mr. Moore. They represent the views of this party. If there are persons who have voted illegally, if there are persons who conspired to commit fraud in the last general election or in any other general election, we say such persons should be named and punished to the full extent of the law. On the other hand, if these allegations are not true they should be proven untrue in order that the good names of the unions and of the elected members of this party from British Columbia may be cleared of the allegations made by Mr. Turner on February 22.

speechtext: I am rising on a point of order. My point of order is this. The hon. gentleman rose on an alleged question of privilege. A question of privilege has to affect the house or some member of the house. But the author of this article has indicated clearly that he is making no accusations against the house or any member of it.

subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS-ARTICLE IN VANCOUVER "PROVINCE" RESPECTING FRAUDULENT VOTING
speechtext:
May I read again to the hon. member the following words:
In every riding where this has been proved to happen, the N.D.P. has benefited, with or without that party's knowledge.
I can see no reason why the Minister of Transport should attempt to resist an investigation into these allegations. If any member of this party or of any other party in the house has been elected by fraudulent means, either with or without his knowledge, this house and the country have the right to know. This attempt to muddy the waters by bringing in something, coming from the Minister of Transport, irrelevant has a very strange aroma.
I wish to move:
That the chief electoral officer be requested to investigate the charges of irregularities in the federal election of 1963 made by Ormond Turner in the Vancouver Province of February 22, 1965, and in any subsequent issues thereof, and to make a full report thereon.

Order, please. I have to determine whether there is, in the Chair's opinion, a prima facie case of privilege and whether to put this motion to the house for the house to decide. It does seem to me, in accordance with citation 104 subsection 5 of Beauchesne, that a matter of this sort must be raised at the earliest opportunity and a prima facie case must be made out; and privilege, of course, relates to the rights, security, dignity and freedom of the members in this particular instance.

It seems to me that this motion is more in the nature of a request for a general inquiry, and that in order to constitute a question of privilege per se with which this house should concern itself at the moment, these charges should be made against several members or an individual member and there should not be a general, blanket charge; because laws are provided in this country to deal with fraudulent elections. It does seem to me also that if the hon. member wishes a general inquiry into a matter like this, the proper procedure would be to make a substantive motion, after due notice.
Therefore, without taking further time of the house, it seems to me that there is no reason to put to the house, for its decision, the motion as suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam; and I see no particular question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, may I make a few comments on this question, and I do so because I have never felt so upset as I am at the present moment. This is not a matter of privilege. I have had the honour of standing for election to parliament, both provincial and federal, 11 times, and I have had the honour to be elected 11 times. The nearest I ever came to defeat was a margin of 3,000 votes. In the federal election in 1963, however, with a total vote for myself of just less than 13,000, I had a majority of 7,000 over the next candidate.
Nine members of this party are from British Columbia. There appears in the press in Vancouver a statement that six of those nine members are here by fraudulent methods.

subtopic: SUGAR BEETS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICE

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: SUGAR BEETS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past three years sugar beets grown in Canada have been supported under the Agricultural Stabilization Act on the basis of $13.72 per standard ton of beets.
I am pleased to announce that for the 1965 crop year the stabilization board has been authorized to support sugar beets at $14.35 per standard ton. This is 104 per cent of the base price or ten year average. This higher support for our beet growers will be provided by means of a national deficiency payment program. In accord with recommendations of the Canadian sugar beet producers association the program will be based on the London daily price of sugar, thus protecting Canadian producers against downward fluctuation of the world sugar market.
I should point out that while the program will assure on a national basis a minimum average return of $14.35 per standard ton of beets, under certain conditions average returns to producers would be above this level.
This is assuming that growers negotiate contracts with processors essentially comparable with those in effect over the past years. I might add that the government is working toward development of a national sugar policy which it hopes in due course will bring a new degree of stability to our sugar beet industry.

subtopic: SUGAR BEETS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has heard the minister at last announce the stabilizing price proposed by the government with regard to the sugar beet industry. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that last year while the price of sugar was so high and consumers were paying top prices, the opposition urged the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time, so far as the international market was concerned, to enter into an international commodity study with the commonwealth sugar producing nations to see if long term contracts could not be arranged in order to assure the sugar beet growers of this country that the price they would receive for their product would be fair and equitable, and that at the same time
Support Price jor Sugar Beets consumers of sugar would not have to pay top prices for this commodity. We were afraid that the very thing that has happened would occur, that the bottom would fall out of the sugar market and that growers of sugar beets in this country would be placed in an intolerable position economically. This is exactly what has taken place.
I know the sugar beet growers have made representations to the government on several occasions over the last few months in order to have a substantial subsidy applied to this crop. It is to be hoped that the price of $14.35 will be sufficient to keep the industry in business. It is far less than the growers asked for, but it is to be hoped it will encourage the sugar beet growers to go on producing for one more year.
This announcement, Mr. Speaker, is a prolongation of the policy of the Conservative party which members of the present government said in 1962 and 1963 was an insult to the sugar beet growers of Canada. Once more the government has held out the carrot that they are undertaking a study to develop a national policy. We feel some disappointment that at this very crucial time in the sugar beet industry, a farming industry in which some $300 million is invested and which produces $35 million to $40 million worth of sugar at wholesale price each and every year, is faced with this thin thread of tenability. The farmers will accept the price of $14.35 a ton, but if the farmers themselves feel it is not enough the result will be that in many instances there will not be enough tonnage attracted to keep the necessary factories in operation. I feel that the government could have done much better than the subsidy of $14.35 announced today.

subtopic: SUGAR BEETS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICE

Mr. Speaker, we are far from satisfied with the support level that the minister has just announced to the house. The price of $14.35 per ton is an increase of only 63 cents over the support price for last year. While I have not been able to do the calculations, I am not sure that the increase of 63 cents per ton even reflects the substantial increase in the selling price of sugar during the last two years.
I also wish to point out that under the Agricultural Stabilization Act no payments have been made to sugar beet producers for the 1962 or 1963 sugar beet crops. We are interested to note that the government is working toward the development of a national sugar beet policy, but I must say

Questions
that we are at least ten years later than most other countries in the world in this regard.
Over the years Canadian sugar beet producers have been forced to compete with the lowest price of sugar anywhere in the world. By the way, Mr. Speaker, only about 10 per cent to 12 per cent of the total sugar production is surplus production, and it is with the price for this sugar that Canadian sugar beet producers have had to compete. The time is long overdue for the government to establish a sugar beet policy to protect part or all of our home market so far as the price at which surplus sugar throughout the world is sold is concerned. I could go into a very long discourse as to what should be done in this respect. We are happy with the increase of 63 cents per ton, inadequate though it may be, and I certainly wish the minister success in coming forward very soon with a national sugar policy that will put some stability under the price that our domestic producers receive for their product.

3.	What was the situation in regard to the use of documents in the case of Professor James Eayrs when he was preparing his book on the history of the Department of External Affairs?
4.	What was the situation with regard to the use of external affairs material in the case of Terrence Robertson in preparation for his book entitled "Crisis"; the inside story of the Suez conspiracy?
5.	Was Mr. Robertson given a greater freedom in use of departmental materials than has been available to other scholars and writers?
6.	Was any correspondence entered into on behalf of Mr. Robertson from anyone in order to facilitate his access; if so, by whom and on what dates?

speakeroldname: Mr. Sianley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS DOCUMENTS FOR RESEARCH
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	The latest amendment to this instruction is dated October 18, 1961. It provides in general that applications for access to official files must be routed through the under secretary of state for external affairs and that permission for access to classified documents will be granted only in exceptional cases to scholars and only when it is clear that the

projects to be undertaken would not be detrimental to the current conduct of Canada's external relations and would in fact be in the public interest (for example, if accounts already published in other countries inadequately presented the Canadian position in regard to the topic of study). Naturally, communications from other governments or belonging to them may not be published without their permission. This directive does not prevent background conversations or interviews with officers of the department on specialized historical topics.
3.	Professor Eayrs was not given access to the files of the department in the preparation of his book on the history of the Department of External Affairs entitled "The Art of the Possible" published in 1961. He had worked on the Mackenzie King papers, by arrangement with the literary executors as assistant to the late Professor R. MacGregor Dawson, and thus had access to certain documents in that collection during work on the preparation of the official biography.
4.	Mr. Terence Robertson was given assistance in 1963 and 1964 in the form of briefing by Canadian officials and others acquainted with the Suez situation. In this process he was given access to certain material of an official nature dealing with particular matters on which he had secured material from foreign sources.
5.	The Department of External Affairs has co-operated with a number of scholars and writers over the years on a variety of projects. It is, however, not possible to make valid comparisons between one such project and another.
6.	Mr. Robertson and his publishers approached the Prime Minister and the Department of External Affairs for assistance. In accordance with normal departmental practice, messages were sent from officials to the Canadian missions he was visiting abroad, requesting them to give the appropriate assistance to Mr. Robertson. The Department of External Affairs is reviewing its policies on these matters and is considering the staffing and administrative requirements which would allow it to be of greater assistance to those doing serious work in the field of international affairs.

speechtext:

In the normal dosage used for humans these drugs are considered to be safe for use at the discretion of the physician.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO STEEL PRICE INCREASE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO STEEL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
May I direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister, and ask him if he has received a telegram from Mr. William Mahoney,

Inquiries of the Ministry Canadian director of the united steelworkers of America, contending that the increased price of steel implemented by the Steel Company of Canada is both unjustified and inflationary? May I ask if Mr, Mahoney has asked the government to investigate the whole question of this increased price of steel, particularly in view of this company's high profits, which have gone up from $21 million to $43 million between 1957 and 1964, and also to ask if Mr. Mahoney has urged the government to step in and prevent any further increases?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO STEEL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
I have received such a telegram from Mr. Mahoney, and he has made a request for a full scale public inquiry such as my hon. friend has just mentioned. I believe I should say in connection with this matter, and I shall be replying in this way to Mr. Mahoney, that we all recognize of course that any change in steel prices is of importance because steel is such a significant item in the cost of manufacture in so many products. I think we also all recognize that the government has no legislative authority to control prices or wages.
In order to keep this matter in perspective, as indeed Mr. Mahoney tried to do in his message, it is important to note that steel prices have changed very little for many years. There has been no general increase since 1957. The increases announced as yet, at any rate, apply only to some steel products and average about 4 per cent. They cover about 22 per cent of the domestic shipments of steel.
I think it is also pertinent to recall that since 1957 the wholesale price index has gone up 8.2 per cent and the consumer price index 12.2 per cent. Therefore the situation as it is at the moment does not, in the government's view, warrant a request to the company to postpone the price increases here and now. But, Mr. Speaker, we agree this situation is of such economic importance that it should be kept under close review, and the government's view which I have just mentioned does not rule out the possibility of either making a request or initiating an inquiry if the situation should develop in a way that calls for reconsideration of the position I have stated.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO STEEL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
As a supplementary question, in view of the fact that this company's profits have doubled in the seven year period, in fact more than doubled, would the Prime Minister not consider whether some investigation would be warranted into the justification for these steel price increases, particularly having ref-

erence to the effect they may have on the whole economy?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO STEEL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I admit that is a very pertinent factor in the whole consideration of the question, as is the fact that hourly earnings in the primary steel industry have risen by 26.5 per cent in that period.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked a question of the Secretary of State regarding the projected activities of the B and B commission, and he informed the house that it should be directed to the Prime Minister. speechtext:

I would hope that the interim report of the commission, which I believe is to be tabled tomorrow and made available to hon. members, will remove some of my hon. friend's fears about unfavourable consequences from the work of the commission.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED PAYMENTS FOR ANIMALS DESTROYED
speechtext:
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce forwarded to me a copy of the resolution related to the question asked yesterday. I find that the resolution was received from the county council of Grey county requesting that consideration be given to increasing the compensation payable under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act for grade cattle from $70 to $100 per beast and for purebred cattle from $140 to $200 per beast. Resolutions supporting the representations from Grey county have been received also from the county councils of Oxford and Ontario.
I should like to point out that under our area testing programs for brucellosis and tuberculosis, the test is conducted at the request of the majority of owners in an area. It is designed to assist livestock owners in eliminating diseased animals from their herds, thus making them more productive. In providing this compensation to livestock owners, it has never been considered that the compensation would fully cover any loss which the owner might sustain but rather was to assist him in the purchase of replacement cattle. It should be noted that the owners of animals ordered slaughtered under the above programs are entitled to the salvage carcass value which, when added to the compensation, represents a sizeable sum. I may say, however, that these rates of compensation are under constant review by my department.

subtopic: NATO-POSSIBILITY OF WITHDRAWAL FROM NUCLEAR ROLE BY CANADIAN FORCES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NATO-POSSIBILITY OF WITHDRAWAL FROM NUCLEAR ROLE BY CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext: My question is one for the Minister of National Defence-I have sent him notice-but in his absence I will address it to the associate minister or to the Prime Minister. Is the Canadian government giving consideration to the major redeployment or switch within NATO which is advocated by the British white paper on defence with a view to limiting nuclear defences; and is the Canadian government planning to withdraw Canadian forces having a nuclear role as part of this process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATO-POSSIBILITY OF WITHDRAWAL FROM NUCLEAR ROLE BY CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
I presume this question is based on a report appearing in a morning newspaper concerning the publication of the British white paper on defence. We are of course giving consideration to all the important questions facing the NATO alliance at the present time. These questions include strategy and future force goals which have been and still are being actively considered by members of the alliance. I think it would be quite misleading, however, to forecast any major redeployment in the near future. What


is occurring is a change in emphasis to reflect changes in the balance of power and in the strategic situation which have occurred in the last ten years. The British white paper seems to reflect this trend, which has already been set out in our own white paper of last March. The hon. member will recall that our white paper forecast a diminution of our nuclear involvement, particularly in the strike role, and an increasing emphasis on conventional capability.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-136. When the committee rose last evening clause 2 was under discussion.
On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last night I was saying that 20

years after the coming into force of this legislation, the actuaries expected a contribution of about 4 per cent from the employees, which represents in fact a kind of tax on all salaries below $5,000, as well as a similar contribution from employers.
The economic consequences for the whole of Canada must be considered in particular when a thorough study is made of the employer's contribution. I appreciate that the benefits paid will be adjusted according to the cost of living index at the time, but the cost of living for the population as a whole will increase considerably through the 4 per cent contribution made by the employer.
The employer's contribution will inevitably lead to an increase in the cost of living index, an increase which will be borne by the whole population because some people will not get anything out of that plan, as was made clear on several occasions.
Therefore, the economic impact will certainly be felt, and rather harshly in the case of many people who in many instances will be unable to benefit from the pension plan but who will still have to face an increase in the cost of living.
On that subject, experts, actuaries in particular, have told us, in many instances, that a large scale pension plan or social insurance scheme, if you prefer, would have necessarily to take into account a great many factors.
To be realistic, one must consider that in 1990 or in 1985, that is in 20 years from now, through automation and cybernetics, the number of workers will no doubt be lower than it is at this time in proportion to the population of Canada. That means that the number of contributors will be less while the number of beneficiaries will be larger through immigration and natural population growth.
To be realistic, it seems to me that one should not go by the workers' and the employers' contributions alone to set up a really great social security plan to provide for those who, some day, will have to retire from work, but consideration should be given also to the situation that will prevail at that time for workers of 45, 50 or 55 years of age.
At the request of our neighbour country, experts in automation submitted a report last fall stating that the effects on the economic factors and the economic life in the United States would be greater following the use of machines and automation than the consequences and effects of the war of 1939-45.

We should, therefore, bear in mind that similar effects will hit Canada, but to establish a plan based solely on contributions paid by the wage earner is not very realistic.
It has also been pointed out that a truly social security plan should take into account many factors. It should, among other things, take into account the value of the dollar today and the value it will have in the future.
Now, I am pleased to quote what the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) said yesterday about the value of the dollar. He stated, as reported on page 11658 of Hansard of February 23, 1965:
Suppose a young person comes into the scheme at 25 and contributes for 40 years. The dollar, declining at the rate I have mentioned, would be worth about 25 cents by the time he was 65. In other words, a person who puts money in at a certain figure would be drawing out dollars which are only about 25 per cent of the value of the dollars he put in.
In this connection, he has stated previously:
Here is a dollar. I have it in my hand. Today, that dollar is worth 100 cents. If we go back over the years we find that the value of the dollar in terms of its purchasing power has declined to the extent of about 21 per cent per year.
I will also quote what the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said concerning the value of the Canadian dollar, as reported at page 11660 of Hansard:
I have been interested in this subject ever since I came to this House of Commons in 1945. On March 30, 1950, I made a speech in relation to the then old age pension legislation. At that time I took some care to do some research as to the purchasing value of the dollar. According to a table which was presented to me by some well informed individuals, based on the purchasing power of the dollar in 1939 as being 100 per cent, the purchasing power of the dollar in 1820 was two dollars and fourteen point six cents. In 1964, in relation to this table, the purchasing power of the dollar was approximately 50 cents.
I am happy to say, although some may think that the proposals we have set forth in view of establishing in Canada a real social security plan would entail a runaway inflation, that two other political parties in this house at least admit that our present financial system is an inflationary system, because there is practically a difference of $2.50 between the purchasing value of the Canadian dollar of 1820 and that of 1964.
Judging by the rate at which the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar devaluated over the past 25 years, we can readily see what it will be in another 25 years.
Therefore, in order to be practical, in establishing a plan we have to take into account many economic factors. The devalua-
Canada Pension Plan
tion of our dollar in our present financial system should also be taken into account.
I recall very well, and those who unreservedly support this pension plan probably do so also, the double talk of the former minister without portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) over the television, the full pages of advertisement during electoral campaigns where the people were warned against the threat of inflation which the monetary theory advocated by Social Crediters would bring about. This is an acknowledgement, by the Conservatives as well as by the members of the New Democratic party or, at least, by certain of their members, that the Canadian dollar is following an inflationary trend never seen before.
It is the present system then that is inflationary. In the pension plan before us, it would be imperative then to take those factors into consideration.
We must keep in mind also that the world's productivity will increase more and more.
The Canada economic council in its recent report, pointed out that the primary goal to achieve is full employment in Canada. Full employment is perhaps the most difficult dream to bring about. This full employment objective is undoubtedly the result of the visionary ideas praised so eloquently by Canadian socialists as well as by "Beveridgian" socialists.
So, I feel that a contributory and compulsory pension plan, that is the Pearson-Lesage plan, if you want to call it that, should be scrutinized before being adopted, and I think that we are about to create the most monstrous administrative organization ever to be seen and which, once again, will overburden the small wage earner, for whom we are supposed to set up social security programs likely to protect him in his old age. subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not taken part in the discussions on this very important piece of legislation up to the present moment, and I had not intended to do so at this stage. As one can well imagine I have followed the deliberations of the committee with considerable interest, and I was rather envious of the fact that I was not able to be a member of that committee, because we all felt that those members were engaged in pioneering in the field of social welfare legislation. I have long been interested in the subject both inside and outside this house.
The reason I rise to speak briefly now is that I have gained the impression from listen-

Canada Pension Plan
ing to the debate that the legislation is not living up to the high hopes that I for one, and I think many others in the country, had anticipated from it. For those who have been interested in social welfare measures over the years there has been much discussion around the point that our social welfare program had fundamental inadequacies and gaps. This resulted from the fact that social welfare in Canada has largely been established upon what might be called a jerrybuilt structure. It has come together in bits and pieces as a result of hasty adjustments to the urgency of the immediate rather than the careful consideration of long term problems. In other words, the programs have been implemented from the standpoint of vote getting procedures rather than dealing with the fundamental changes in social structure and organization which have occurred in Canada, and indeed throughout the whole civilized world, during the past three decades. For those who have followed the problem over the past three decades, and even longer than that because these changes actually began in the wake of world war I, the record is well known.
When this legislation was first introduced into the house, as I listened to the remarks of the minister as she commented upon the mark I version of the pension plan I came to the conclusion that this was the ultimate solution to the fundamental problem which has existed in our welfare program. As a member of the former Conservative administration I know that this was the approach we took in tackling what we regarded as the last major inadequacy in our social welfare program, the provision of financial security and an adequate income for those least able to look after themselves. I refer, for example, to survivor benefits for dependants which up to that time were and still are a major gap.
Unfortunately the government has proceeded with unseemly haste and it is only after the many suggestions that have been put forward in the house, the excellent suggestions that have been put forward by the various provincial governments when they have been belatedly consulted by the federal government and also, of course, after the excellent work of the committee that we have a piece of legislation that has come a long way from the initial presentation. As has been said by most speakers during this debate, in my view the officials deserve a great deal of credit for the marvellous job they have done in bringing the present order
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
out of the initial chaos, but they can only do so much.
As one who did not have the opportunity to sit in on the discussions of the committee but who has read the voluminous reports of their proceedings, I can see that responsible groups such as the Canadian Welfare Council and the Canadian Association of Social Workers are still concerned over the fact that the legislation before us, even though it is going to cost billions of dollars, even though it is going to raise the taxes of every Canadian by 3.8 per cent on top of the other tax exactions for pension and welfare programs, does not come to grips with the basic inadequacy in all our welfare programs, namely the problem of the low income group, the people who actually need this sort of security. I think anyone who is interested in social welfare benefits will agree that all a government social welfare program can do is to ensure a certain level of financial security. It is not social security or social welfare in the broad sense because social welfare in the broad sense can only come from the functioning of our basic social institutions.
Certainly this is a point that must have been brought before the government because I recall reading a speech on the subject of social welfare in Canada made on September 15, 1959, by the then editor of the Winnipeg Free Press, Mr. Tom Kent, in which he referred to the real problems of welfare as non-material misery. He was dealing with the real social needs as distinct from the financial needs to which I referred a moment ago. He also referred to the subject of preventive welfare, programs designed to meet basic welfare needs. The legislation before us obviously does not meet those intangibles in social security programs. It is merely a program designed to ensure certain financial and income benefits to a broad cross section of the Canadian public and unhappily it once again perpetuates the basic inadequacy of not meeting the needs of what are sometimes referred to as chronic indigents.
Actually the reason I decided to speak was that the parliamentary secretary to the minister spelled out in some detail, as reported on page 11642 of Hansard for yesterday, that the government understands it is not meeting this problem. He was replying to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi who had dealt with the difficulty of pauperism and chronic poverty. The parliamentary secretary said:
I do not believe this question should be raised when we are discussing a wage related contributory pension scheme.

It is spelled out there that this fundamental gap remains, even though we are moving into a new era of social welfare that, as I have already intimated, will build up multi-billion dollar funds, will result in increases in taxation and will have all sorts of ramifications throughout the whole economic structure of Canada. In my own province, for example, it is estimated that the tax of 3.8 per cent which will be required to provide the funds to cover the wherewithal for these pensions will involve the sum of $36 million which would represent a sales tax of about 4 or 5 per cent. Up to the present time Manitoba is one of two provinces, the other being Alberta, that have been able to avoid the imposition of a direct sales tax. It is for this reason that the premier of Manitoba has consistently put forward the viewpoint that in moving forward in a massive way in this legislation we must be sure we are dealing with first things first.
I am not going to go over the ground that has been covered already by several spoke-men of this party and the views which were put forward in the committee in some detail by members of the Conservative party. They spelled out this difficulty in quite specific terms. As I read the committee reports, they put forward amendment after amendment which were promptly voted down by the committee. Having listened to the discussion and having read the record, it is apparent that the whole objective of these amendments was to meet this basic gap in our social welfare program in order to cover those who are actually in need of financial assistance.
Someone has referred to the legislation as upside-down welfare. It gives the most to those who need it the least. Two and a half million Canadians will not be covered in any shape or form by any financial benefit under this legislation. Therefore I can only conclude that the fanfare which has greeted this legislation indicating that it is the consummation of the Canadian welfare structure has unfortunately been saturated with the same political overtones that have unhappily been present in all previous Canadian welfare programs.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take up any more of the time of the committee, except to re-emphasize that Canada needs a co-ordinated social justice program. This plan does not meet that criterion. I hope, even at this late date, as has been suggested by other members who have spoken, the government will still consider bringing forward some amendments or adopting others which have 20220-740
Canada Pension Plan
been put forward in concrete terms on several occasions by members of the Conservative party. It is hoped that the government will accept these amendments so that we will get the kind of program the propaganda indicated we were going to receive. I feel it is important this be done while the bill is under discussion because it is going to be a long, long time before a piece of legislation as important as this one is up for discussion again.
As I read the committee report, and as I examine the bill, which is complex and difficult for one who was not in the committee to comprehend, there are safeguards in the bill which make future major changes to the plan extremely difficult. I noticed, for example, that changes can only be effected with the approval of two thirds of the participating provinces and then only if they represent two thirds of the population of Canada. It is for this reason I make this final appeal to the government to make sure that the initial plan is the best possible plan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, may I assure the government and the minister that I do not intend to speak at length. As many hon. members on this side of the house have already pointed out, there are some weaknesses in this bill. I propose to touch on a few more and ask a few questions I should like to have cleared up.
First of all, I should like to congratulate the committee members who worked so hard during the recess. I understand they had 51 meetings and heard a great deal of evidence, some of which was quite detailed. In fact, the whole bill is one of the most complex pieces of legislation to be introduced in the last few years. One of the things which immediately comes to mind when discussing this pension plan is, how much is it going to cost? Some of the evidence that was presented to the committee dealt with that question in this way: It was stated the cost would be similar to increasing the average income tax now paid by 23 per cent, a substantial amount in my opinion. Another way of looking at it according to some evidence presented is that it would be the same as imposing a sales tax of 4 per cent or 5 per cent, again a substantial amount.
As soon as one realizes that it is going to cost quite a bit, he immediately asks, as many people across Canada have been doing, who is going to benefit? Will they benefit? The previous speaker pointed out, and I wholeheartedly agree with him, that a great

Canada Pension Plan
many people will not receive any benefit from the plan, because of their situation. Some of them, of course, find themselves in this situation through no fault of their own. It is too bad that this whole area has to be left out of this pension plan. It is too bad that the pension plan could not be an all-encompassing welfare and social improvement plan of some sort.
When one considers that this plan will be compulsory, he immediately thinks of those people who are already paying into a registered pension plan. In some of the evidence it was suggested that 30 per cent of the working force is now paying into a registered plan of one kind or another. The Ontario brief suggested that 60 per cent of the working force of Ontario now has the right to join a registered pension plan. Of course anyone who is self-employed may join a pension plan on an individual basis with any of the companies that are in the business of selling these plans. The vast number of people who are not likely covered by a pension plan today will be the ones missed by this pension plan. I am thinking particularly of the self-employed, the small farmer, who perhaps may not have a net income of $800. I know this amount must appear rather small to many hon. members. However a great many farmers throughout Canada, not only in eastern Canada and Quebec, have a net income of less than $800 after expenses have been considered. These people will be missed by this plan.
There is one other aspect of the plan that I find disappointing, namely that it is not actuarially sound for any of the persons paying into it. Surely if we are going to leave out those people who cannot afford to pay into it, then those who are paying into it should not be getting a bonus, as is the case for certain groups under this plan. If you are going to give one group in our society a bonus, then I do not believe you have any sound argument for leaving out another class altogether and giving them no chance to participate. I do not really understand the reasoning behind these provisions. I am quite disappointed. I favour a pension plan; I know it has many good points to it, such as portability. Why bring in a pension plan which will give bonuses to some and prohibit others from participating at all? I find this difficult to understand.
I should like to return to a consideration of the farmers for a moment. I am concerned about a situation which may well arise under which a farmer will be paying into the

pension plan. He will have a net income of well over $800. He will be paying into the pension plan on a monthly basis, and then along will come a hailstorm and wipe him out completely. In that year in which he is already paying into the plan, he will not have a net income of over $800. I may be wrong, but it is my understanding that on April 30, or whatever the checking up date for the year may be, he will make out a form which will state his net income was below $800 in that year. He will then have to ask for a refund of the money he has paid in, and that year will be called a no income year and will not be taken into account in averaging his earnings.
Suppose a farmer is now 55 years old. Many people in that age group are not participating in pension plans at present, and such a farmer will want to qualify each one of the remaining ten years in order to take full advantage of the Canada pension plan at age 65. Then, suppose that in three or four of those years he is hailed out. He may be willing to pay his contributions to the plan but, because he does not have a net income of $800 during those three or four years, he is prohibited from making contributions to the plan.
I know parts of my constituency which in four out of five years crops have been completely hailed out and in the following year they produced champion wheat kings at the Toronto royal winter show. If this pension plan were actuarially sound there would be no harm in allowing a farmer, who is capable and willing, to pay contributions into it, even though he does not have the minimum income required under the terms of the plan.
I would like the minister to correct me if I am wrong but, as I read the bill, if a farmer pays into the pension plan in a given year, and in the fall of that year his crops are completely hailed out, that year is deducted from the permissible years over which his pension is paid and averaged.

speechtext:
I would like to indicate one or two things in this regard. First of all, a farmer would pay his pension contributions at the same time as he pays his income tax, which is in December and April, so that he would not make a payment for the year 1966 until December 1966 and thus he would know what his situation was before he made his payment.
The second point is that although there is no averaging provision, and I would like to deal with this in more detail when we come to a certain clause in the bill, if we take the

case of a farmer who is 55 years of age and he is hailed out one year during the next 10 years, if he continues to farm between the ages 65 and 70 he could pick up that year by continuing to work until he is age 66, contribute in that year, and then take his pension.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: As I understand the minister, a farmer will not pay into the pension plan every month?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: It will be twice a year, when he pays his income tax.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I am firmly convinced most farmers pay income tax only once a year. However, would he still have to make monthly deductions for his hired help?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Yes, if it were permanent hired help and did not come within the exemptions in the bill, 25 days or $250. For permanent hired help earning over $600 he would have to contribute.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Then that would get away from his paying in only once a year to the fund at the time when he pays his income tax, and would still exclude those years in which he was hailed out from being pensionable years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: There is the dropping out after the 10 year maturity period and, as the hon. member pointed out earlier in his statement, a person who is 55 years of age and starts paying into the pension plan will, because of the very nature of the plan, enjoy some great advantages. Then, after the 10 year maturity period there is the dropout period, which is presently in the bill at 10 per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Dealing with the minister's reference to a farmer working on past 65 or 70, as I understand it he has the option to work on past 65 but he must take the pension after 70. I do not think farmers are a particularly hardy breed but many of them work on past 70, and I wonder if it is necessary to have so severe a penalizing clause in the bill if they continue work after 70.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
There is no penalty for working on beyond 65, except that between 65 and 70 if you have a certain amount of income the amount of pension you would draw would be reduced, or if you have a large amount of income you would continue to contribute. But for each year that you contribute between the age of 65 and 70 you can drop out one of your low income years. If a farmer continues to farm after 70 years he would be getting the maximum pension to 20220-740J
Canada Pension Plan
which he is entitled under the bill, as well as his income from other sources.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: He can earn as much as he likes after 70?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Without having anything deducted?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Then I was wrong. I was under the impression that there was a penalizing clause and a limit to the amount one could earn even after 70 years of age.
Though I support the bill I am disappointed in it. The coverage it provides is not as wide as I would like and I really see no reason why a farmer, earning less than $800 net income a year, should not be permitted to make contributions for that year if he wishes. I do not think he could be forced to contribute but I do not see why he is prohibited and I would like the minister to consider this matter.
I recognize that a portable pension scheme will eventually become a good thing for Canada but I had hoped we could be assured it will be portable in all provinces. Apparently we will not know that until 30 days after the bill is passed because the provinces have 30 days in which to announce their intentions of entering the pension field on their own. Only then will we know whether their pension plans will coincide with this one, and they must coincide in order to make the scheme fully portable.
Many people have been wondering how existing pension plans will be integrated with this one. The Canada pension plan is not actuarially sound but private plans are, and this will cause a great deal of difficulty. Quite a number of people will be paying into two pension plans. It is true they will reap the benefits of both plans, but we are a young country which needs to be developed. We should not be enjoying the luxury of saving so much for our old age when there is so much needed to be done with the money we earn during our working life.

speechtext:
At the conclusion of my remarks I intend to move a formal amendment to clause 2, and I might explain briefly that the amendment proposes to add a definition of the word "resident" to the clause. The definition will define a resident as a person who fulfils the residence qualifications of subsection (1) of section 3 of the Old Age Security Act.
I should like to explain briefly the reason for moving such an amendment at this time. There is no residence qualification as such in the bill before us. I think the basic reason is that employment has to be in Canada and therefore the question as to residence has not concerned those who drafted the bill. However, we intend to propose later on, certain substantive amendments to various clauses which would add as beneficiaries persons who will have made a smaller contribution than the one envisaged or, in some cases, no contribution at all to the fund. In these circumstances we feel the benefit of such a provision should be limited to residents of Canada as they are defined in the Old Age Security Act. We propose to add

certain benefits. I will list them as four in number. First, we intend to add words to the effect that for the purposes of benefit under this act those who earn less than $600, or $800 as the case may be-the minimum provided by the plan-shall be included. At the present time the minimum amount of $600 in respect of employed persons represents the dividing line. If people earn less than $600 in any year they are not required to make any contribution to the Canada pension plan and are entitled to no credit. But if they earn more than $600 they have to pay only in respect of the amount which exceeds $600. We feel this is unfair to those people who are in the very low income brackets. We feel that in this type of measure there must be a certain element of welfare and we intend to include these people to the extent which our amendments will make clear. Our proposal will be that any person who earns less than $600 in any one year shall be entitled to file a return of his earnings as usual and take credit for the amount of his actual earnings, but will not be required to make any contribution for that year. We feel this will have two results. First, it will help those who consistently earn less than $600 to get a pension and, second, it will keep the average lifetime earnings of those who are earning incomes around the $600 figure at a reasonable amount; in no year would they be classified as having received no earnings where in fact they have earned $400 or $500, for example. We shall include these people as beneficiaries under the plan and we shall pay them when they retire the minimum pension of $25 a month, provision for which is made in one of the later clauses. We feel this group of people cannot in any case afford to make contributions.
We intend, in the second place, to provide minimum pensions of $25 on retirement. As the plan is presently drafted, a person with marginal lifetime earnings might receive at the age of 65 a pension as low as $10 or $15 a month-an income so low in relation to his requirements that he would need assistance from other sources. We feel that if people have paid even minimal amounts into the plan during their working lives, they should be entitled to a minimum pension, and we believe the minimum they should receive is $25 a month. There may be people who have made very small contributions because they have consistently earned less than $600 a year. Nevertheless they will be entitled to the

minimum pension. In this way we intend to bring such people within the pension plan, no matter how small their income, and pay them a minimum of $25 a month. We think this is only fair to those who have made contributions to the national economy all their lives, particularly when their earnings have fallen within the very low income brackets.
We have also decided to provide for minimum pensions for people presently over 70 years of age who would not have the right to benefit from the plan in normal circumstances. We feel that there will be a great gap between those who reach 70 years of age and have been on the pension plan and those who are too old now ever to get on it. We believe that these people are entitled to be classified as contributors to the pension plan by reason of their contribution to the economy of this country in past years. This is why we are moving to bring into this particular clause a residential requirement, because we do not feel that a person should be entitled to come here from another country and take advantage of our minimum pension. He should have made his lifetime earnings in Canada, have resided here and contributed in some way to our national economy.
We are proposing that this minimum of $25 per month should be paid out of the Canada pension plan. In this way we differ to some extent with the proposal put forward by other members who are suggesting an overall increase in old age security. We are also proposing that persons between 65 and 70 who have made no contributions and are unable to do so, or who have made very small contributions for a very short period of time-those persons who may now be approaching the age of 65 and may not be able to contribute in any great amount-also be provided with a minimum pension of $25 per month which will go beyond and above the old age security that has been described. Here again, Mr. Chairman, we feel that this will do something to fill the gap in regard to those people who are now between 60 and 65 and will not have the opportunity of contributing to this plan for any great period of time. If those people who are now 63 contribute for two years, they will be able to draw a pension of roughly $20 per month; if they have contributed for just one year, they will be able to draw a pension of about $10 a month. We intend to include those people in the minimum pension provisions and classify them as contributors. Later on in the proceedings we intend to define the group of people whom I have just described
Canada Pension Plan
as contributors, and they will be deemed to be contributors under the provisions of the Canada pension plan. But this does not come within the clause that we are now considering. As I stated, Mr. Chairman, all these people whom we are adding are people who will derive a greater benefit than would normally be the case with a wage related plan. For that reason we believe they should be Canadians, and for that reason we are adding this definition at this time.
It may be asked, can we afford to pay these funds out of the Canada pension plan as it is presently established? Mr. Chairman, the answer to this question is yes. At a later date, when we make our substantive amendments to later clauses, we will be presenting to the committee our exact amendments and will then be setting out in detail the financial implications of our amendments. But at this moment let me say that we have calculated and have had calculated the effects on the Canada pension fund of all our amendments. In the first few years it will constitute a fairly heavy drain on the funds, but it will at no time overdraw or nearly overdraw the funds. Most of the figures that have been given to the special committee and to the house take the year 1970 as a standard year when the initial transition period will have passed. We find that, even after paying the additional benefits that we are proposing, in that year alone there will be an accumulation of between $75 million and $100 million.
The effect of our amendments will be to slow down the growth of this fund. There will be a transition period of 20 years in accordance with our proposal, and this will have some effect on the fund in the later stages. There is also another feature that we are going to introduce, namely that of collecting from those earnings over $600 a year on the basis of their whole earnings up to the maximum in the bill while not collecting at all from those who earn less than $600 a year. This particular feature will raise, in the year 1970, approximately $107 million to offset the cost of the proposals we are making.
As I stated, Mr. Chairman, the fund will grow more slowly in the early years as the result of accepting our proposals; but it will accelerate in the later years because, first, all those who are now 65 and over who will receive a benefit, without contribution, under our plan, will gradually be replaced by those who have contributed to the fund in the normal way. In other words, our provisions are transitional and will be replaced in due course by people who have contributed to the pension

Canada Pension Plan
plan in the normal way and will draw benefits in the normal way. So that after this transition the fund will start to grow more quickly. Second, our proposal to extend the transition period from 10 to 20 years will not be effective to any great extent in the first few years; that is to say, by 1970. But as the years go on, between the tenth and twentieth years it will have a very substantial effect on the growth of the fund and the fund will continue to grow from those years forward.
I have indicated in a general way that we are satisfied that these proposals can be handled out of the Canada pension fund, at no time putting the fund in danger. For those reasons, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley:

"(cc) "resident" means a person who fulfils the residence qualifications of subsection (1) of section 3 of the Old Age Security Act".

Mr. Chairman, the amendment which has been placed before this committee is a very fundamental amendment which would change the nature of the bill before us. It is not just a mere amendment to the definition clause; it is the basis on which subsequent amendments, as indicated by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, will change a piece of social legislation which is intended as a social insurance measure, as my hon. friend from Halifax indicated yesterday, into something quite different, something which would have very serious effects on national unity in Canada, since its application could only apply to that part of Canada which was not contracting out. It would also have very serious effects on the nature of the fund itself.
There are three fundamental ways in which we in Canada, as other modern nations, enact social measures which have generally been described, in a rather confused way, by spokesmen for the opposition as welfare measures. The most ancient of these, one which is very important in our structure, relates to social assistance. When we speak of welfare, traditionally social assistance based on a test of individual means or of income or of resources, or various combinations of those, has been the usual way of approaching it.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the rather touching appeal of the hon. member-and I remember the one made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi yester-

day-concerning poverty in the rural regions. Equally I have learned of the cases of poverty which exist in our urban parts of Canada. I also listened to the hon. member for Northwest Territories who told us of the very deep poverty of many of the native peoples of this country whom he represents in this house. But at that point, Mr. Chairman, I realize that the proper measures to deal with this question must be related to social assistance.
Another method of approach is the universal benefit method, which usually requires a test not of individual resources but of residence. The amendment offered to the committee very significantly deals with residence and does not deal in any way with the concept of public assistance; nor is it related to social insurance as such. Fundamentally this is a measure which defines eligibility not in terms of individual requirements based on case work, not in terms of universal benefits, but in terms of contribution, and contributory records. The purpose of this legislation is to take pensions out of politics. This amendment I suggest would put pensions more deeply into politics than they have ever been in the history of this country.
I think we have seen in recent years the record of competitive bidding between the major political parties, each trying to arrive at some pension level which could be defended in some way as adequate, although governments have wisely refrained from trying to label any benefit method they have chosen as an adequate benefit. In proposing this legislation the government had in mind the fact that in Canada there is the same variation in requirements between urban and rural communities, between highly industrialized provinces and the less industrialized provinces, between those with higher standards of income and the income levels of those with lower standards. The intention clearly was not to deal with the acute problem of rural poverty, for which ARDA, for example, is designed. It was not to deal with the urban poverty problem, which has to be tackled through revision of our public assistance legislation and standards. The intention was to deal with the problem of portable pensions of wage earners in urban and industrialized communities, who obviously needed something in addition to the flat rate benefits of a universal plan if they were to retire with a sense of dignity. This legislation is designed as a measure of social insurance, and hon. members opposite have been attacking it in an attempt to say that the plan has not done the very things it was not intended to do.

It is not an instrument by which we are heading an attack on rural poverty. It is not an instrument by which I submit we race in a cavalier fashion, and I suggest an irresponsible and cynical fashion on the part of members of the opposition who have espoused the doctrine which first came from that corner of the house, and with a good deal more conviction, toward $100 a month at age 65. Members in other parts of the house, in an obvious attempt to gain political capital, are now applying the same doctrine which was used with regard to the unemployment insurance fund, where $1 billion in the unemployment insurance fund was drained away to nothing in a period of six years. They have applied the same philosophy to a measure of social insurance in which the same principle of funding, which is fundamental to such measures, would be adopted.
